Lessons.Title: Finding and Interpreting Inverse Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: find and explain inverses of linear functions involving multiple arithmetic operations, interpret units/domains and check the composition in both directions. First-party Edulytiks adaptation from Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 4 Lesson 16, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/4/16/preparation.html and student tasks https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/4/16/index.html (CC BY 4.0). Publisher Building On HSA-CED.A.2/HSA-CED.A.4 and Addressing HSA-CED.A.4/HSF-BF.B.4.

Original bookshop model T(n)=9n+5 dollars for n nonnegative whole-number books: $9 each and a one-time $5 delivery fee. Given bill T, solve n=(T−5)/9, but only bills of 5+9n for nonnegative integer n correspond to complete book purchases. A $50 bill implies n=(50−5)/9=5 books; $51 would imply 46/9 books and is not admissible under this model.

A familiar temperature relationship, Celsius C to Fahrenheit F, is F=(9/5)C+32. Reverse steps by subtracting32 then multiplying5/9, so C=(F−32)×5/9. Check0°C↔32°F, 100°C↔212°F, 40°C↔104°F. The mathematical inverse changes both units and input/output roles.

Student task: solve two multistep equations for input variables, create a two-column forward/inverse data table, distinguish mathematical inverse from physically admissible purchases and evaluate if a function is one-to-one. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct isolation, two-way checks, units/domain reasoning and appropriate contextual interpretation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reverse order
KeyConcepts.Definition: Undo the final operation first, then earlier operations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse domain and range
KeyConcepts.Definition: The inverse's valid input values are the original function's attainable outputs.
KeyConcepts.Example: T(n) has bills {5,14,23,...}, not every real bill.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two-way verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: Check both original(inverse(y)) and inverse(original(x)) where defined.

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve for book count
WorkedExamples.Question: A $50 total follows T=9n+5. Find n.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use an original function and check its rule, inverse, constraints, and units at multiple inputs.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 5 books; inverse n=(T−5)/9 on attainable bills.

WorkedExamples.Title: Invert Fahrenheit conversion
WorkedExamples.Question: Find Celsius equivalent of 104°F.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use an original function and check its rule, inverse, constraints, and units at multiple inputs.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both directions restore values and units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify unattainable bill
WorkedExamples.Question: Could $51 be an exact T(n)=9n+5 for integer n≥0?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use an original function and check its rule, inverse, constraints, and units at multiple inputs.
Steps: This is not a whole number.
The model only permits integer book counts.
So $51 is not in the purchase-total range.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, not an attainable bill under the model.
WorkedExamples.Check: Nearest five and six books cost $50 and $59.

CommonMistakes.Correction: Subtract the fixed fee before dividing.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming every real output can be inverted into a physically valid count
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Integer input constraints limit output range.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check inverse result is nonnegative integer.

SummaryPoints: Linear inverse rules reverse the original operations in order.
A book-price inverse can produce an inadmissible fractional count.
Fahrenheit/Celsius conversion is reversible by solving for C.
Teacher verifies checks, units and contextual domain.
